141.event_title: Edward VIII abdicates to marry Wallis Simpson
141.event: King Edward VIII wished to marry Wallis Simpson, an American who was still married to her second husband, Ernest Simpson, when the king's attachment to her became a matter of state; she obtained a preliminary divorce decree only in October 1936. As head of the Church of England, the king faced firm opposition from Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin's government and the Church to his marrying a divorced woman whose former husbands were living, and Baldwin rejected a proposed morganatic marriage. Edward abdicated in December 1936, telling the nation by radio that he could not carry out his duties without the help and support of the woman he loved, and his brother became King George VI.
141.explanation: Edward had been raised from birth to understand the duties and public role of the crown, yet he gave up the throne rather than give up a woman who had been another man's wife.
141.tie_back: The kural says the folly of desiring another man's wife is not found in those who truly understand virtue and worldly affairs; Edward's choice cost him the very position his whole training had prepared him to fill.
141._accuracy_note: A reasonable but partial fit: Wallis Simpson was legally another's wife during the courtship, but Edward acted openly and sought marriage, and whether his choice was folly is a matter of opinion.

142.event_title: Publius Clodius is caught in Caesar's house during the Bona Dea rites
142.place: Rome, in the official residence of Julius Caesar as pontifex maximus
142.event: The rites of the Bona Dea, a festival from which all men were excluded, were held that year in the house of Julius Caesar, and the young aristocrat Publius Clodius Pulcher entered disguised as a woman musician. According to Plutarch he was seeking Caesar's wife Pompeia; he was recognised by his voice, the rites were halted by Caesar's mother Aurelia, and he was found and driven out. Clodius was tried for sacrilege and escaped conviction, reportedly through bribery, while Caesar divorced Pompeia.
142.explanation: The scandal became one of the most notorious in Roman history, exposing Clodius to prosecution and public ridicule and creating lasting enmities, notably with Cicero, who gave evidence against him.
142.tie_back: The kural calls the man who lingers at another's door for his wife the most foolish of all wrongdoers; Clodius was literally caught inside another man's house, disguised and exposed.
142._accuracy_note: A strong and almost literal fit for the image of the man at another's door, though his motive rests on ancient reports, and this event is also used once elsewhere in the book from Caesar's side.

143.event_title: Richard Wagner and Cosima von Bulow
143.place: Munich, Bavaria, and Tribschen near Lucerne, Switzerland
143.event: Cosima von Bulow, a daughter of Franz Liszt, was married to the conductor Hans von Bulow, one of Richard Wagner's foremost champions, who conducted the premiere of Wagner's Tristan und Isolde in Munich in 1865. Cosima's relationship with Wagner began while she was still married to Bulow, and she had children with Wagner during the marriage; in 1868 she left her husband and went to live with Wagner at Tribschen in Switzerland. Bulow granted her a divorce in 1870, and she married Wagner later that year.
143.explanation: The affair is one of the best-known episodes in musical history, remembered partly because the man betrayed was a friend who had devoted his talents to Wagner's work.
143.tie_back: The kural condemns those who plot against the household of people who trust them; Bulow had welcomed Wagner into his professional and domestic life and was deceived within it.
143._accuracy_note: A strong fit for betrayal of a trusting friend's household, though Wagner and Cosima later married and the kural's verdict of moral death is the commentary's, not history's.

144.event_title: The O'Shea divorce case ends Parnell's leadership
144.event: Charles Stewart Parnell, leader of the Irish Parliamentary Party, was at the height of his popularity and often called Ireland's uncrowned king when Captain William O'Shea filed for divorce from his wife Katharine at the end of 1889, naming Parnell as co-respondent. The case was not defended and the divorce was granted in November 1890. When Parnell refused to step down, Gladstone made clear that the Liberal alliance would end, the Catholic hierarchy declared against him, and in December 1890 most of his party withdrew from his leadership; he died in October 1891 still fighting to regain it.
144.explanation: The split divided Irish nationalism and damaged the cause of Home Rule for years, showing how one private choice could undo a great public career.
144.tie_back: The kural asks what a man's greatness is worth if he enters another's home for his wife; Parnell's immense standing proved worthless once the affair became public.
144._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of greatness made worthless by this one lapse, though some historians stress the political motives behind the divorce case.

145.event_title: Georges d'Anthes and the duel that killed Pushkin
145.event: Georges d'Anthes, a French officer serving in Russia, openly courted Natalya Pushkina, the wife of the poet Alexander Pushkin, and in 1836 anonymous letters mocking Pushkin over his wife circulated in St Petersburg. D'Anthes married Natalya's sister Ekaterina in January 1837, but the gossip continued, and later that month the two men fought a duel in which Pushkin was mortally wounded; he died two days later. The tsar stripped d'Anthes of his military rank and expelled him from Russia.
145.explanation: Russia lost its greatest poet, and in Russian memory d'Anthes has been remembered ever since chiefly as the man who killed Pushkin.
145.tie_back: The kural warns that the man who thinks it easy to cross into another's household earns a disgrace that never dies; d'Anthes' pursuit of Pushkin's wife left his name permanently tied to that loss.
145._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for undying blame, but d'Anthes went on to a successful career in France, so the lasting disgrace lies mainly in Russian memory.

146.event_title: Alexander Hamilton publishes the Reynolds Pamphlet
146.event: In 1791, while serving as the first US Secretary of the Treasury, Alexander Hamilton began an affair with Maria Reynolds, a married woman. Her husband, James Reynolds, then demanded money to keep quiet, and Hamilton paid him, including $1,000 in two instalments by January 1792. When a journalist accused him in 1797 of illegal speculation with Reynolds, Hamilton published a pamphlet confessing the affair and the blackmail in order to clear himself of financial wrongdoing; the revelation humiliated his family and ended any hope he had of becoming president.
146.explanation: Hamilton cleared his name of corruption only by publicly confessing a private wrong, and the affair shadowed the rest of his career.
146.tie_back: The kural names enmity, sin, fear and disgrace as the four companions of the man who transgresses against another's home; Hamilton met all four, from the husband's hostility and years of fear of exposure to lasting public disgrace.
146._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's four companions, documented in Hamilton's own published confession.

147.event_title: The Hongzhi Emperor keeps Empress Zhang as his only consort
147.event: The Hongzhi Emperor of the Ming dynasty, who reigned from 1487 to 1505, kept Empress Zhang as his only wife from his time as a prince until his death, although Chinese emperors customarily kept many consorts. His ministers repeatedly urged him to take more consorts to secure the succession, and he refused. Historians describe him as the only monogamous emperor in Chinese history.
147.explanation: In a court where an emperor's household was expected to include many women, Hongzhi defined his own household by fidelity to one wife.
147.tie_back: The kural identifies the true householder as the man who does not desire a woman who belongs to another; Hongzhi went further and refused even the consorts his position allowed.
147._accuracy_note: A strong fit for the faithful householder, though the kural speaks of not desiring another's wife, and historians link Hongzhi's choice partly to the dangers of the harem in his childhood.

148.event_title: Goethe leaves Wetzlar and Charlotte Buff
148.event: In the summer of 1772 the young Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, then a trainee at the Imperial Chamber Court in Wetzlar, fell in love with Charlotte Buff, who was already engaged to Johann Christian Kestner. After a few months Goethe left Wetzlar abruptly in September 1772 without saying goodbye, and Charlotte married Kestner the following spring. Goethe drew on the experience for his novel The Sorrows of Young Werther, published in 1774, in which Lotte was modelled on Charlotte and her fiance on Kestner.
148.explanation: Rather than press his feelings on a woman promised to another man, Goethe withdrew, and the episode became the seed of one of the most influential novels of the age.
148.tie_back: The kural calls it the greatest manliness not even to look with desire at another's wife; Goethe's departure from Wetzlar was a withdrawal from a woman who belonged to another.
148._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Charlotte was engaged rather than married, and Goethe had already pursued her for months before he withdrew, so the restraint was late and partial.

149.event_title: Charles and Emma Darwin's marriage at Down House
149.event: Charles Darwin married his cousin Emma Wedgwood on 29 January 1839, and in 1842 they moved to Down House in Kent, where they raised their children and lived for the rest of his life. Emma supported his scientific work, handled correspondence for him, and nursed him through long periods of ill health. Their marriage lasted 43 years, until his death at Down House in 1882, and English Heritage describes it as very happy and loving.
149.explanation: Darwin's steady family life at Down gave him the security in which he carried out decades of research, and his marriage is remembered as a model of companionship.
149.tie_back: The kural says that those who do not embrace another's wife are worthy of every good thing; Darwin's long, faithful marriage was accompanied by a full family life and a lifetime of honoured work.
149._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it shows the blessings of a faithful marriage, but no documented temptation was resisted, and the kural's claim of desert is moral, not historical.

150.event_title: Ulysses S. Grant's lifelong devotion to Julia Dent Grant
150.place: St. Louis, Missouri, and elsewhere, United States
150.event: Ulysses S. Grant married Julia Dent in 1848 after an engagement of four years delayed by the Mexican-American War, during which he wrote her many letters. In 1854 he resigned suddenly from the army amid reports that he had begun drinking heavily while separated from his family, and he then failed as a farmer and in several other jobs before the Civil War. Through these setbacks and his later fame as general and president, the couple remained devoted; the National Park Service describes their long marriage as marked by love, trust and respect.
150.explanation: Grant's career included real failures and a reputation for drinking, yet his loyalty to his wife was never in question, and his letters to her are preserved at the Library of Congress.
150.tie_back: The kural says that even a man who falls short in many ways should at least not desire another's wife; Grant, whatever his failings, held firmly to that line.
150._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Grant's failings were mostly misfortune rather than wrongdoing, and the evidence is of devotion rather than of a temptation refused.
